title: Trunk Port in Wrong Access VLAN
symptom: Host on VLAN 10 cannot ping the server that is also expected to be in VLAN 10. Other hosts on the same access switch reach the server fine.
topology_note: Two access switches connect to a distribution switch. PC_A is in VLAN 10 and server ServerX should be in VLAN 10. Both are physically connected to the same access switch.
expected_fault: The switch access port that plugs into the server is assigned to VLAN 20 instead of VLAN 10, so the server is isolated from VLAN 10 hosts.
expected_fix: Verify the access VLAN assigned to the port with show interfaces switchport | confirm the current access vlan; reassign the port with switchport access vlan 10; verify with show vlan brief; then test connectivity again with ping from the host.

title: No Inter-VLAN Routing
symptom: Hosts on different VLANs cannot ping each other. Hosts within the same VLAN can ping each other successfully.
topology_note: A single access switch carries VLAN 10 and VLAN 20. PCs in VLAN 10 and PCs in VLAN 20 cannot communicate with each other. There is no router or Layer 3 switch providing routing between the VLANs.
expected_fault: Inter-VLAN routing is not configured, so traffic between VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 has no router to forward it.
expected_fix: Confirm there is no router or SVI providing Layer 3 routing between the VLANs with show ip route; configure inter-VLAN routing either using a router-on-a-stick with subinterfaces or a Layer 3 switch with SVIs; verify by pinging between VLAN hosts.

title: New Port in Mismatched VLAN
symptom: A newly added PC has no connectivity even though it was configured with a valid IP address. The PC cannot reach the gateway or any other device.
topology_note: A network administrator adds a new PC and plugs it into an access switch. The PC is configured for subnet 192.168.30.0/24, but the access port it is connected to is assigned to VLAN that maps to a different subnet.
expected_fault: The access port is statically assigned to a VLAN whose corresponding IP subnet does not match the IP configuration of the newly added PC.
expected_fix: Check the VLAN assigned to the access port with show vlan brief; confirm the IP subnet used by that VLAN; move the port to the correct VLAN with switchport access vlan <correct_vlan>; verify connectivity with ping.

title: PC Missing Default Gateway
symptom: A PC has a valid IP address but cannot reach any device outside its own subnet. It can reach hosts only on the local LAN.
topology_note: The PC is configured with an IP address and subnet mask but the default gateway field is empty. There is a router on the LAN providing the gateway for that subnet.
expected_fault: The default gateway is missing on the PC, so the PC does not know where to send traffic destined for other subnets.
expected_fix: Open the PC IP configuration with ipconfig; add the correct default gateway (the router interface address for the subnet) in the PC network settings; verify by pinging a device on a remote subnet.

title: Wrong Default Gateway Address
symptom: A server can reach hosts on its own subnet but cannot reach any device outside the subnet. Ping to the gateway itself also fails.
topology_note: The server is configured with a default gateway that points to an IP address that is not a router interface (a non-router address, such as another host or an unused address).
expected_fault: The server default gateway points to a non-router address, so the server cannot forward traffic to other subnets.
expected_fix: Check the configured default gateway with ipconfig; identify the correct router interface address for that subnet with show ip interface brief; update the server gateway; verify remote connectivity with ping.

title: Duplicate IP Address on Two Hosts
symptom: One host intermittently drops off the network. Network connectivity is unstable and unpredictable.
topology_note: Two PCs on the same subnet are both configured with the same static IP address. When both are powered on, the network experiences address conflicts.
expected_fault: Two hosts are configured with the same static IP address, causing an address conflict and unstable connectivity for both.
expected_fix: Identify the duplicate IP by checking ipconfig /all on the affected hosts; change one host to a unique unused IP address within the subnet; confirm uniqueness; verify stable connectivity by pinging each host.

title: DHCP Pool Exhausted
symptom: Clients on the DHCP network receive no IP address and default to an Automatic Private IP Address (169.254.x.x). They cannot reach the network.
topology_note: A DHCP server is configured with a limited address pool for a subnet that has more clients than available addresses. New clients cannot obtain an address.
expected_fault: The DHCP address pool has run out of available addresses, so new clients cannot obtain an IP lease and fall back to APIPA.
expected_fix: Check current leases with show ip dhcp binding and the pool size with show ip dhcp pool; determine if the pool is exhausted; either expand the pool range or reduce the number of clients; release unneeded leases with clear ip dhcp binding; verify a new client obtains an address.

title: DHCP Assigning Wrong Subnet
symptom: Clients receive an IP address from DHCP, but the address is in the wrong subnet and they cannot reach the intended network resources.
topology_note: The DHCP server pool is configured with a network and mask that does not match the subnet where the clients actually reside.
expected_fault: The DHCP pool is configured for the wrong network range, so clients in one subnet receive addresses from a different subnet.
expected_fix: Inspect the DHCP pool configuration with show ip dhcp pool and show running-config; compare the pool network with the client subnet; correct the pool network and mask; verify a client receives an address in the correct range with show ip dhcp binding.

title: DHCP Relay Not Forwarding
symptom: Clients on a remote VLAN receive no DHCP address and default to 169.254.x.x, even though a DHCP server exists on another VLAN.
topology_note: There is a DHCP server on VLAN 10 and clients on VLAN 20. The router interface for VLAN 20 has no DHCP relay configuration, so client requests are not forwarded to the server.
expected_fault: The VLAN 20 router interface has no ip helper-address pointing to the DHCP server, so DHCP broadcast requests are not relayed to the server on VLAN 10.
expected_fix: View the VLAN interface configuration with show running-config; confirm there is no ip helper-address on the client VLAN interface; add ip helper-address <dhcp_server_ip> to the VLAN 20 interface; verify clients obtain an address.

title: DNS Server Unreachable on Client
symptom: A PC can ping devices by IP address but cannot resolve hostnames. Name resolution fails for all names.
topology_note: The client is configured with an IP address for a DNS server, but that DNS server is unreachable from the client LAN (wrong IP or the server is down). Ping to the DNS server IP fails, while other remote IPs succeed.
expected_fault: The DNS server IP address configured on the client is missing or unreachable, so the client cannot perform name resolution even though IP connectivity exists.
expected_fix: Check the configured DNS server with ipconfig /all; ping the DNS server IP to confirm reachability; correct the DNS server address to a reachable server; verify name resolution with nslookup.

title: Wrong DNS Server Address
symptom: All name resolution lookups on the client fail. The client cannot resolve any hostname to an IP address.
topology_note: The client is configured with a DNS server IP that does not actually exist or is not a functioning DNS server on the network.
expected_fault: The client points to a nonexistent DNS server IP address, so all name resolution requests fail.
expected_fix: Check the DNS server address with ipconfig /all; confirm the correct DNS server IP from the network administrator; update the DNS server configuration on the client; verify resolution with nslookup.

title: Missing DNS A Record
symptom: One specific hostname cannot be resolved, while all other hostnames on the network resolve correctly. Name resolution for the affected name returns an error.
topology_note: The DNS server is reachable and resolving other names correctly, but the A record for a particular host has not been added to the DNS zone.
expected_fault: The DNS A record for the requested hostname is missing from the DNS server, so that specific name cannot be resolved even though the DNS server is functioning.
expected_fix: Run nslookup for the failing hostname to confirm it does not resolve; verify the DNS server is reachable by resolving another known name; add the correct A record for the hostname on the DNS server; verify resolution again.

title: Missing Static Route
symptom: Two directly attached networks cannot reach each other, even though they are connected to the same router.
topology_note: Router1 connects to network 192.168.10.0/24 and network 192.168.20.0/24, but there is no static route configured to connect the two remote networks beyond the directly connected ones.
expected_fault: A required static route is missing on the router, so packets destined for the remote network are not forwarded.
expected_fix: View the routing table with show ip route to confirm the destination network is absent; add the missing static route with ip route <dest_network> <mask> <next_hop>; verify the route appears with show ip route and test connectivity with ping.

title: Wrong Next-Hop in Static Route
symptom: Packets are dropped at the router and never reach the destination network, even though a static route exists for that network in the routing table.
topology_note: Router1 has a static route for network 192.168.30.0/24, but the next-hop address configured in the route points to a nonexistent or incorrect neighbor.
expected_fault: The static route points to an incorrect next-hop address, so the router cannot forward packets for that destination network.
expected_fix: Inspect the route for the destination network with show ip route; confirm the next-hop is reachable and correct; correct the next-hop in the static route configuration; verify traffic flows by pinging the remote network.

title: Dynamic Route Not Advertised
symptom: A network that should be reachable via a dynamic routing protocol is absent from the routing table, so devices cannot reach it.
topology_note: Router1 is running a dynamic routing protocol (such as RIP or OSPF), but the network statement for one of its directly connected networks is missing from the protocol configuration.
expected_fault: A network statement is missing from the dynamic routing protocol configuration, so that network is not advertised and is absent from neighbor routing tables.
expected_fix: Check the routing table with show ip route to see the missing network; review the routing protocol configuration with show running-config; add the missing network statement to the protocol; verify the route is advertised by checking neighbor routing tables.

title: Route Preference Conflict
symptom: Traffic takes an unexpected path to a destination network, causing poor performance, even though a route to the destination exists.
topology_note: Router1 has both a static route and a dynamic route for the same destination network, but the wrong one is preferred due to administrative distance, so traffic uses the undesired path.
expected_fault: Conflicting static and dynamic routes exist for the same network, and the router prefers the wrong path because of administrative distance.
expected_fix: Inspect the routing table entry for the destination with show ip route to see which route is preferred; review the administrative distances; remove or adjust the conflicting route to make the intended path preferred; verify traffic uses the correct path with traceroute.

title: ACL Blocking All Host Traffic
symptom: A particular subnet cannot reach a server at all. All traffic from that subnet to the server is blocked, even though other subnets can reach it.
topology_note: An extended or standard access list is applied to a router interface in front of the server, and its rules are too broad, denying all traffic from the affected subnet.
expected_fault: The access list has a deny statement that is too broad and blocks all traffic from the affected subnet to the server.
expected_fix: Review the access list rules with show access-lists; check how many packets match the deny statement; refine the ACL to permit the required traffic while still applying any intended filtering; reapply the corrected ACL and verify connectivity.

title: ACL Blocking Only One Service
symptom: ICMP ping to a server works, but HTTP (web) access to that same server fails.
topology_note: An access list applied on the router permits ICMP but denies TCP port 80, blocking only the HTTP service while other traffic is allowed.
expected_fault: The access list denies only TCP port 80 (HTTP), blocking web access while permitting other traffic to the server.
expected_fix: Review the access list with show access-lists to confirm it denies TCP port 80; add a permit statement for the required web service appropriately; reapply and verify HTTP access succeeds.

title: ACL on Wrong Interface or Direction
symptom: Traffic is being blocked when it should not be, or traffic that should be filtered is passing. The filtering behavior is unexpected.
topology_note: An access list was created correctly, but it was applied to the wrong interface or in the wrong direction (inbound instead of outbound, or on the wrong interface in the path).
expected_fault: The access list is applied to the wrong interface or in the wrong direction, causing unexpected traffic filtering behavior.
expected_fix: Review where and in which direction the ACL is applied with show ip interface; confirm the intended interface and direction; remove the misapplied ACL and apply it to the correct interface/direction; verify expected filtering behavior.

title: NAT Inside/Outside Not Assigned
symptom: Hosts on the inside network cannot reach the outside network even though NAT is configured with a translation rule.
topology_note: A router has a NAT/overload rule configured, but the ip nat inside or ip nat outside command has not been applied to the relevant router interfaces.
expected_fault: The ip nat inside or ip nat outside interface assignment is missing, so NAT translations are not performed for traffic crossing the router.
expected_fix: Check NAT translations with show ip nat translations and the interface configuration with show running-config; confirm the inside and outside interface assignments; apply ip nat inside to the LAN interface and ip nat outside to the WAN interface; verify hosts can reach the outside.

title: NAT ACL Does Not Match Inside Subnet
symptom: Only some hosts on the inside network can reach the outside network successfully, while others cannot.
topology_note: A router uses an access list to define which inside addresses are eligible for NAT. The access list matches only part of the inside subnet, leaving some hosts untranslated.
expected_fault: The NAT access list does not match the full inside subnet range, so only the matched addresses are translated and the rest cannot reach the outside.
expected_fix: Review the NAT access list with show access-lists and show ip nat translations; identify which addresses are being translated; correct the access list to match the entire intended inside subnet; verify all inside hosts can reach the outside.

title: Static NAT Wrong Mapping
symptom: An internal server cannot be reached from the outside network, even though a static NAT entry exists for it.
topology_note: A static NAT rule maps an outside global address to an inside server, but the inside local address or global address is configured incorrectly.
expected_fault: The static NAT mapping points to the wrong inside local or outside global address, so outside users reach an incorrect or nonexistent server.
expected_fix: View the static NAT translations with show ip nat translations and the config with show running-config; verify the inside local and global addresses; correct the static NAT mapping to point to the intended internal server; test outside access.

title: Wireless Clients Get No IP
symptom: Wireless clients can associate with the access point but do not obtain an IP address, so they cannot access the network.
topology_note: An access point offers an SSID, but the wireless network is either not linked to a DHCP-enabled VLAN or DHCP is not being served for the wireless clients.
expected_fault: The SSID is mapped to a VLAN that has no DHCP service, or the wireless network lacks DHCP, so clients associate but receive no IP address.
expected_fix: Check whether wireless clients appear in show ip dhcp binding; confirm the SSID-to-VLAN mapping and that a DHCP pool serves that VLAN; configure a DHCP pool for the wireless VLAN or map the SSID to the correct VLAN; verify clients receive an address.

title: Wireless Wrong SSID or Security
symptom: Wireless clients either cannot join the SSID or cannot reach the LAN after joining, while other wireless clients work.
topology_note: An access point has multiple SSIDs; one SSID is mapped to the wrong VLAN or uses a security key (WPA) that does not match the clients.
expected_fault: The SSID is mapped to the wrong VLAN or a WPA security key mismatch prevents clients from joining or accessing the LAN.
expected_fix: Review the access point configuration with show running-config to inspect SSID-to-VLAN mapping and security settings; correct the SSID mapping or security key; verify wireless clients associate and reach the LAN.

title: Interface Administratively Down
symptom: A connected link is down, and the interface state shows administratively down/down. The remote device also shows the link as down.
topology_note: A switch or router interface is connected to a device, but the interface contains the shutdown command in its configuration.
expected_fault: The interface has the shutdown command applied, placing it in the administratively down/down state.
expected_fix: Check the interface state with show ip interface brief to confirm administratively down/down; remove the shutdown command with the no shutdown command; verify the interface state changes to up/up; confirm connectivity with ping.

title: Intermittent Physical Link
symptom: A link is physically down with no link light on either device, so no connectivity exists between two devices.
topology_note: Two devices are connected by a cable, but the link is not established. Possible physical cause is a wrong cable type or the cable is not fully connected to the port.
expected_fault: The link cannot be established due to a physical connectivity problem, such as the wrong cable type or a port that is not connected properly.
expected_fix: Check the port status with show interfaces status to confirm it is down; physically verify the cable type and that both ends are connected to the correct ports; replace with the correct cable if needed; verify the link comes up.

title: Interface Up/Down Due to Duplex Mismatch
symptom: A link is up on the port but the protocol is down, showing an up/down interface state, so traffic cannot traverse the link.
topology_note: Two directly connected devices have a duplex mismatch: one is set to full duplex and the other to half duplex, causing constant collisions and preventing the link from working reliably.
expected_fault: A duplex mismatch between the two connected device ports causes the interface to stay in an up/down state and prevents traffic from flowing.
expected_fix: Check the duplex settings and interface state with show interfaces; confirm both ends use matching duplex settings; configure both ends to the same duplex or auto-negotiation; verify the interface state becomes up/up and traffic flows.

title: Trunk Not Passing VLANs
symptom: VLAN data from hosts on one switch is not reaching hosts on another switch. Traffic within a single switch works, but not across the link between switches.
topology_note: Two access switches are connected by a link, but the link has not been configured as a trunk, or the trunk does not allow the required VLANs.
expected_fault: The link between the switches is not configured as a trunk (or does not allow the required VLANs), so VLAN traffic cannot pass between the switches.
expected_fix: Check trunk status with show interfaces trunk to see if the link is a trunk and which VLANs are allowed; configure the link as a trunk with switchport mode trunk and ensure the required VLANs are in the allowed list; verify VLAN traffic passes between switches.

title: VLAN Mismatch on Trunk
symptom: Some frames are dropped between two switches across their trunk link, so hosts in the affected VLANs cannot communicate across the link.
topology_note: Two switches are connected by a trunk, but the allowed VLAN list or native VLAN does not match between the two ends, causing frames in certain VLANs to be dropped.
expected_fault: The trunk allowed-list or native VLAN configuration does not match between the two switches, causing frames in mismatched VLANs to be dropped.
expected_fix: Compare the trunk configuration on both switches with show interfaces trunk; check the allowed VLAN list and native VLAN; make the two ends consistent; verify frames pass for the intended VLANs.

title: Subnet Mask Mismatch
symptom: Two hosts that appear to be in the same IP range cannot ping each other, even though their IP addresses fall in the same subnet.
topology_note: Host A and Host B are on the same physical LAN. Host A uses a /24 mask and Host B uses a different mask, so they do not compute the same network, and they cannot communicate directly.
expected_fault: The two hosts use mismatched subnet masks, causing them to compute different networks even though their IPs overlap.
expected_fix: Compare the IP addresses and subnet masks with ipconfig /all on both hosts; set both to consistent, correct subnet masks for their shared network; verify the hosts can now ping each other.

title: Host IP in Wrong Subnet
symptom: A host cannot reach other devices on its LAN, even though the network appears configured correctly, because its IP address falls outside the intended subnet range.
topology_note: A host is configured with an IP address from a different sub-block than the rest of the devices on its LAN segment, so it is effectively on a different subnet.
expected_fault: The host is assigned an IP address from a different subnet than the rest of the LAN, so it cannot communicate with its intended neighbors.
expected_fix: Check the host IP with ipconfig /all and compare it to the planned subnet; assign the host a valid IP within the correct sub-block; verify connectivity by pinging neighbors on the LAN.

title: Missing SVI on Layer 3 Switch
symptom: One VLAN on a Layer 3 switch cannot be routed to other VLANs, while other VLANs route between each other correctly.
topology_note: A Layer 3 switch has SVIs (VLAN interfaces) configured for several VLANs to provide inter-VLAN routing, but the SVI for VLAN 30 is missing.
expected_fault: The VLAN interface (SVI) for VLAN 30 is missing on the Layer 3 switch, so VLAN 30 cannot be routed to other VLANs.
expected_fix: Check the VLAN interfaces with show ip interface brief to confirm no SVI exists for VLAN 30; create the SVI with interface vlan 30 and assign an IP address in the correct subnet; enable or ensure routing is active with ip routing; verify inter-VLAN routing for VLAN 30.

title: Missing Router Subinterface on Router-on-a-Stick
symptom: One VLAN on a router-on-a-stick cannot reach the other VLAN subnets, while the other VLAN subinterfaces route correctly.
topology_note: A router is configured with a router-on-a-stick topology using subinterfaces on a single physical trunk link to route between VLANs, but the subinterface for VLAN 30 is missing.
expected_fault: The router subinterface for VLAN 30 is missing from the router-on-a-stick configuration, so VLAN 30 traffic cannot be routed.
expected_fix: Check the subinterfaces with show ip interface brief to confirm no subinterface exists for VLAN 30; create the subinterface with encapsulation dot1Q 30 and assign an IP address in the correct subnet; verify inter-VLAN routing for VLAN 30.
